sections.html:
Visit the Fayette County Recorder at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 305, Washington Court House. Doors are open weekdays from 8 am to 4 pm. The phone is 740-335-1770 and the fax is 740-333-3521. Real estate and personal property records for the whole county are kept here, such as:

  • deeds, mortgages and land contracts
  • IRS liens and mechanics liens
  • plats and zoning resolutions
  • military service discharges

The county seat, Washington Court House, is also the only city in the county. One office records every Fayette County deed, for in-town homes and township farms alike.

Pricing here is a set amount by length, and the first two pages cost the same.

Recording fee by document length
Pages in the documentRecording fee
1 page$39.00
2 pages$39.00
3 pages$47.00
4 pages$55.00
5 pages$63.00
10 pages$103.00

A $4.00 marginal fee may be added. The posted schedule ends at ten pages, so call for a quote on anything longer. Behind the numbers is Ohio Revised Code 317.32: each page carries a base fee and a housing trust fund fee, and a county may also add a document preservation surcharge of up to five dollars for its general fund.

sections.h2: Delivering a deed to the Recorder
sections.html:
Hand the deed in at Suite 305 or send it by mail. Payment is by cash or check, because cards of any kind are not accepted.

  • Papers arriving after 3:30 PM wait until the next day to be run, so a late afternoon drop misses that day's time stamp.
  • To get documents returned by mail, enclose a stamped envelope addressed to yourself.
  • Since June 22, 2026, the county offers e-recording through Simplifile for both conveyance and non-conveyance documents.

Time stamps count because instruments are filed in the order presented, with the exact time noted (R.C. 317.13). When two papers hit the same house, the earlier one has priority.

sections.h2: What the Auditor does before the deed is recorded
sections.html:
Go to the Auditor's real estate department before the Recorder. It handles deed transfers, new parcels, lot splits and homestead exemptions, and it is down the hall at 133 S. Main Street, Suite 303, phone 740-335-6461, on identical weekday hours.

Conveyance paperwork lives on the Auditor's forms page: the Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100), the Exemption from Real Property Conveyance form (DTE 100EX), a statement for homestead property, another for property under current agricultural use valuation, and mobile home forms. Standards for legal descriptions are posted there too.

On the DTE 100 you list total consideration, then subtract what was paid for things that are not real property. The fee is figured on what remains. Questions follow about whether the seller reported senior or disabled homestead or farm use valuation, and whether the buyer will occupy the home by January 1 of the next year. Leaving out the owner-occupancy application holds back the 2.5 percent reduction until a timely, proper application is filed, so complete that section. The Auditor can quote the conveyance fee rate before closing.

Ohio recorders can reject a paper that the law neither requires nor authorizes to be recorded, or one they reasonably believe is materially false or fraudulent. The remedy for a rejected filer is a request to the Court of Common Pleas for an order to record.

One refusal is not optional. R.C. 5301.94 directs the recorder to reject a right-to-list home sale agreement, so an owner pitched on recording one against the house should know the office will not accept it.

Nobody at the counter is obliged to inspect what you hand over. Legal description, names and signatures are the drafter's job to check.

Beyond the recording fee, R.C. 317.32 sets other charges, each split into a base fee and an equal housing trust fund fee:

  • Certified copy of a recorded document: $1 base plus $1 trust fund per page, with a further 50 cents plus 50 cents when the recorder's seal is required.
  • Photocopy outside the recording process: $1 plus $1 per page.
  • Marginal reference entered by a separate instrument: $2 plus $2 for each reference, which matches the $4.00 marginal fee Fayette posts.
  • Local fax or electronic transmission: $1 plus $1 per page.

A title company wants proof of how you took ownership, and the vesting deed shows it. If your own copy is lost, the Recorder can supply one for the per-page copy charge. Sellers most often need a certified copy of their vesting deed, since a title company will often ask for one. Order it a few days before closing so it is in hand when the title agent calls.

sections.h2: Values, tax bills and a sale
sections.html:
The Auditor doubles as chief fiscal officer and real property appraiser. Reappraisal comes every six years under Ohio direction, with an update in year three. The Auditor builds the yearly tax list, then splits what the Treasurer collects among townships, schools and other taxing bodies. Delinquent taxes are certified and published by the Auditor, and the Treasurer chases those accounts.

As secretary of the county Board of Revision, the Auditor also hosts the Board of Revision Property Complaint form on the forms page. A value dispute goes on that form, not to the Recorder. Spot an error in the Auditor's online data for your parcel and you can report it for correction.

When the deed is filed, the conveyance statement has to record whether the seller was asked about a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction and about farm use valuation. Ending farm use can trigger a recoupment charge, which buyer and seller sort out between themselves (R.C. 319.202). If you own farmed acreage, tell the title agent early.

The 2020 count was 28,951 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 28,552. Washington Court House anchors a micropolitan area in the Columbus-Marion-Zanesville region. Madison, Pickaway, Ross, Highland, Clinton and Greene counties touch its borders, and Good Hope and Pancoastburg are the named unincorporated places.

On a cash sale the order of stops is short. Start with the legal description and conveyance forms at the Auditor in Suite 303. Then take the signed deed to the Recorder in Suite 305 before 3:30 PM, with a check or cash for the fee. With no lender involved there is no loan package to deliver, so the deed is often the only document you carry in.

Before you drive over, phone both offices to confirm the fee total and that the legal description is acceptable. A rejected description sends you back to the start, and it is cheaper to catch a problem by phone than at the counter.

faqs.q: How much is the Fayette County recording fee for a two page deed?
faqs.a: It costs $39.00, with a possible $4.00 marginal fee on top. One page is also $39.00, and three pages are $47.00.

faqs.q: Can I pay the Fayette County Recorder by card?
faqs.a: No. Only cash or a check will be taken.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Fayette County?
faqs.a: Yes, through Simplifile, for both conveyance and non-conveyance documents. You can still file on paper at Suite 305.

faqs.q: What time should I get a deed to the Fayette County Recorder?
faqs.a: Aim for before 3:30 PM. Later arrivals are held and run the next day.

faqs.q: Does the Fayette County Recorder or Auditor handle the conveyance form?
faqs.a: The Auditor does, in Suite 303 of the same building. Both the DTE 100 and the exemption form DTE 100EX are on the Auditor's forms page, and the Recorder files the deed afterward.
